# Synopsis

Eleven years, Irena Vasko has read the frontier from the same chained book: left column the state's tongue, right column the traveller's, nothing said that is not printed and numbered, every deviation entered in ink as an unlisted utterance. It is a post that runs on the promise that the phrasebook cannot change — only misread — and Vasko has built her whole discipline, and her silence, on that promise holding. It costs her the ordinary reflex of speaking a sentence that isn't hers to read; she keeps a private tally of everything the book will not let her say. Then, on a night no different from eleven years of them, a traveller named Ana Petrik crosses outbound at 01:40, and at page seventy-four Vasko finds a sixth phrase where five have always stood — printed in the traveller's column, addressed, unmistakably, to the person behind the counter. No rule has been broken. No one has written in the book. Duty officer Tomas Brandt logs the moment exactly as procedure demands and asks nothing further; that is the kindness he believes in. Vasko says the words as printed. Petrik answers as though she had been waiting for them. What follows asks only what any night shift can survive: who is changing a book no one at the post may touch, and why the changes are learning to speak about her. For readers of *Convenience Store Woman* and *The Employees*, who want their uncanny delivered in triplicate and countersigned.


# Chapter 1 — Page Seventy-Four, Phrase Six

At 01:40 the stove pipe was the warmest thing in the building, and Irena Vasko stood with her palms half an inch off it, close enough to feel the heat lift the fine hairs on her wrists.

"It shuts," Brandt said. "It shuts, and then it opens again on its own, and I am not permitted to wire it, because wiring it is a modification." He toed the damper. It rang. "A modification requires a request."

Light came up the pass then, two cones swinging across the block wall, and Brandt was at the ledger before the engine was audible. He uncapped the pen. He wrote the time in ink, the figures square and unhurried, and only then put his hand to the barrier control. Eleven years, and she had never once seen him do it in the other order.

The card came through the window in a gloved hand. Valid, current, the photograph a younger version of the woman now bending to the gap. Vasko drew the chained phrasebook towards her by its cloth spine, the links sliding on the counter, and opened it flat.

"Page seventy-four, phrase one." She read the left column, then the right. Purpose of travel.

"Collection," the woman said. "Ana Petrik. There's a consignment at the depot on the far side and I've been told it's been sitting since Thursday, which I doubt, but I'm told it anyway."

"Page seventy-four, phrase three. Expected duration."

"Two hours there, two back, longer if the road has iced. Call it five." Petrik smiled at the numbering, the way people did, as though it were a game the post had invented for its own amusement.

"Page seventy-four, phrase four. Goods carried."

"Nothing outbound. Paper in the glovebox."

Vasko's eye went down the column to six, and stopped before it read.

She knew the shape of it first. The cadence — the particular short lift at the end, the hesitation built into a clause — was one she recognised the way you recognise a footstep on stairs. She had never read this phrase aloud. It was not on this page. It was on this page now, set in the right-hand column, the traveller's column, and it was phrased to ask something of the person standing behind the counter.

Nothing else was printed there for her to say.

"Page seventy-four, phrase six."

Petrik answered it fully, and a little more than asked, and did not seem to find it strange.

Brandt wrote the numbers into the ledger. The barrier went up, and the tail lights pulled away, and Vasko watched them until the pass took them, and added it to the count of what she was not allowed to say aloud.


# Chapter 2 — The Cupboard Volume

At 03:10 the headlights came up out of the dark the way they had gone down into it, and Ana Petrik put the same card on the counter with the same unchanged purpose written on it in the same hand.

Vasko turned to page seventy-four. Four more phrases in the right-hand column that had not been there, and not only on seventy-four: on eighty-one, on ninety-three, on pages she could have set out from memory. Every one of them addressed the person holding the book. She counted them privately and read them as printed, page and phrase number first, in the flat cadence the licence required.

Petrik answered each in full. She answered the repeated ones too, patiently, unhurried, as though repetition were not an error but the whole of the exercise. Brandt wrote the time, the name, the purpose and the phrase numbers in ink, blotted it, and only then put his hand to the barrier control. The arm went up. The engine noise thinned out along the pass and the post went quiet again, with the wind coming across the block wall in long unbroken pushes.

Vasko opened the counter cupboard. The ledger volumes stood in there in their order, and she took out one from four years back and laid it open beside the chained phrasebook, which stayed on its chain, as it did.

Unlisted utterances, in Brandt's square careful hand, dated. *Translator stated, off page: it is not far now.* She found it printed in the traveller's column of page ninety-three, numbered, tidied — *the distance remaining is small* — the shape of it kept, the roughness taken out. She went back a volume and found another. Then four more. Eleven years of things she had not been able to stop herself saying, standing in the book as approved phrasing for questioning her.

Deeper in the oldest volume the hand changed. Another writer altogether: struck corrections, one line through each, initials pressed so hard the paper had given under them. The entries ran on and then stopped mid-quarter, no closing entry, nothing signed off.

Brandt spoke from the stove without turning round. The quarterly returns went down to the district in the bag, he said, and came back as reissued phrasing. That was how it had always worked. He said the damper wanted seeing to.

No one had written in the book. Nobody here had touched it. She had fed it, accurately, every quarter for eleven years, because Brandt logged her honestly, and Brandt logged her honestly because he believed accuracy was a kindness. She closed the volume and counted that, too.


# Chapter 3 — Page Two Hundred and Twelve

The stove had gone down to embers and the road held nothing. Vasko turned the phrasebook to its last page because there was nowhere else left in it to turn.

Page 212 was headed *Approved Terms of Address*, and the terms were numbered like everything else. She read down the column with her finger not touching the paper. 212.4: *Lenk.* 212.5: *Vasko.*

She counted the entries above and below. Nine in all. Two of them were people she could name.

"Brandt."

He looked up from the stove door.

"The book." Her own words came out the way they always did, short, costing more than they carried. "My name is in it. Printed. As a term of address."

He was quiet a moment. Then: "That's a Form 9. There's no other form for it." He went to the drawer. "It's filed here, it goes down in the bag with the quarterly returns, and it comes back countersigned by the district. Or it doesn't." He set the blank on the counter beside her, square to the edge. He did not offer to recopy it, nor to settle it between them.

She completed it in ink. *Nature of irregularity: an issued document reads other than as printed.* Under the old ledger volume in the cupboard there was a carbon of the same form, eleven years soft at the folds, the hand on it small and even, and Vasko understood while her pen moved that the district had never written back, and that the district's silence was the whole of what the post would ever hold of Dora Lenk. There was nothing else. There was a name on page 212, one line above her own.

Headlights came up the pass at twenty past five.

Same card, same purpose, patiently given. Brandt entered the crossing in the night ledger, time and name and purpose, in ink, before he touched the barrel switch. Vasko put her hand flat on the open book and read the counter questions from page 212, by number, in the flat cadence, including the ones that began with her own name set as the approved way of addressing the woman holding the book. Petrik answered all of them, and more than all of them, and seemed to find the repetition the point.

The barrier lifted. The tail lights went over the crest.

Vasko folded the Form 9 into the district bag with the quarterly returns and drew the cord. Brandt brought the barrier down. She worked the last hour of the shift, and kept the count.
